description: Question: can you know how volatile a liquid is at room temperature from its boiling point alone? Idea: Clausius–Clapeyron with a constant heat of vaporisation gives ln(P/1 atm) = −(ΔS_vap/R)·(Tb/T − 1), and Trouton's rule says the entropy of vaporisation ΔS_vap = ΔH_vap/Tb is nearly the same for every liquid (about 10.5 R ≈ 87 J/(mol·K)), because a mole of vapour at 1 atm is about equally disordered whatever it came from. So on the axes Tb/T − 1 against log₁₀(P/1 atm) every liquid should fall on one line through the origin, and the boiling point alone gives the whole vapour-pressure curve: the reason shortcut distillation design and solvent volatility rankings start from boiling points. Data: every Wikidata substance with a vapour pressure, its temperature and a boiling point (SPARQL, values as entered, converted here from mmHg, torr, kPa, hPa, atm, bar, °F and °C; boiling points at reduced pressure dropped). Polars keeps one reading per pure substance (a SMILES) nearest 25 °C, 10 K or more below its boiling point (326 liquids), backs out the ΔS_vap each reading implies, R ln(P0/P)/(Tb/T − 1), and sorts the liquids by hydrogen-bond donors read from the SMILES. Aha: the 229 liquids without a donor cluster tightly (median 99.3 J/(mol·K) = 11.9 R, middle half 94–105) and one number predicts 84% of their vapour pressures within a factor of 2 across nine orders of magnitude; the 59 O–H donors (alcohols, glycols, phenols, acids) imply 16 J/(mol·K) more (Welch t = 7.2) and evaporate about half as readily as their boiling point suggests, because hydrogen bonds order the liquid (ethanol 119, ethylene glycol 130, glycerol 142). Caveats: the room-temperature constant is above Trouton's 10.5 R because ΔH_vap grows as T falls below Tb (a constant ΔH is an approximation; Watson's correlation fixes it); carboxylic acids dimerise in the vapour, which lowers their ΔS (formic acid 94); Wikidata values are crowd-curated from safety data sheets (NIOSH, ICSC), often rounded ("1 mmHg"), and 11 readings imply impossible ΔS (under 50 or over 200 J/(mol·K): a unit or qualifier error, a solid, a mixture), listed in the data check; the donor class is a SMILES pattern, not a measured property; water has no vapour pressure with a temperature in Wikidata. Next: check the suspect readings against PubChem's experimental vapour pressures; add a second reading per liquid to fit Antoine's equation; compute relative volatilities of pairs (the distillation question) and look for azeotropes where donors meet non-donors.
name: Trouton's rule: the vapour pressure from the boiling point
